brief.scenario: Mr Brian Hollingworth, 62, a retired industrial painter who smokes, was referred with painless visible haematuria. CT urography shows a 3.5 cm enhancing mass in the right kidney and a filling defect in the bladder.
brief.task: Answer the examiner's questions on the referral and investigation of haematuria, and the pathology and management of renal and bladder cancer.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Refer, image, look inside, then two cancers: one kidney, one bladder, each staged and treated on its own merits.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Treating the CT as the whole work-up. The bladder still needs cystoscopy, and 'muscle-invasive means cystectomy' is incomplete.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: "Visible haematuria at 45 or over, without infection, is a suspected cancer pathway referral."

grid.label: Referral criteria
grid.fail: Watches and waits, or orders a urine test and repeats it in a month.
grid.pass: Suspected cancer pathway referral: 45 or over with unexplained visible haematuria without urinary infection, or persisting after treated infection.
grid.high: Adds 60 or over with non-visible haematuria plus dysuria or raised white count; the same visible-haematuria criteria cover renal cancer.

grid.label: Investigation
grid.fail: Relies on the CT alone, or on urine cytology or biomarkers instead of cystoscopy.
grid.pass: Urine dipstick and culture, renal function, CT urography for the upper tracts, and cystoscopy for the bladder.
grid.high: Explains that CT misses flat bladder lesions such as carcinoma in situ; urinary biomarkers do not replace cystoscopy.

grid.label: Histological types
grid.fail: Calls the renal mass a transitional cell carcinoma, or cannot name either type.
grid.pass: Kidney: renal cell carcinoma, mostly clear cell. Bladder: urothelial (transitional cell) carcinoma.
grid.high: Names papillary and chromophobe RCC; links clear cell RCC to VHL gene loss on chromosome 3p.

grid.label: Risk factors
grid.fail: Cannot name smoking as a risk factor for either cancer.
grid.pass: Both: smoking. Bladder: occupational aromatic amines (dyes, paints, rubber). Kidney: obesity, hypertension.
grid.high: Relates them to this patient (smoker, painter); names von Hippel-Lindau syndrome; advises stopping smoking.

grid.label: Non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer
grid.fail: Plans cystectomy for every bladder tumour, or cannot describe TURBT.
grid.pass: TURBT including detrusor muscle, a single intravesical mitomycin C dose at first TURBT, then risk-stratified treatment.
grid.high: High-risk disease: repeat TURBT within 6 weeks, then a choice of intravesical BCG (induction and maintenance) or radical cystectomy.

grid.label: Muscle-invasive bladder cancer
grid.fail: States cystectomy is the only treatment, with no MDT or neoadjuvant therapy.
grid.pass: Specialist MDT. Neoadjuvant cisplatin-based chemotherapy if suitable, then choice of radical cystectomy or radiotherapy with a radiosensitiser.
grid.high: Stages with CT chest, abdomen and pelvis; discusses urinary diversion options and involves a clinical nurse specialist.

grid.label: Renal mass
grid.fail: Plans a biopsy of every renal mass, or radical nephrectomy for all.
grid.pass: Stage with contrast CT chest and abdomen; MDT; partial nephrectomy for a T1 tumour where feasible.
grid.high: Biopsy reserved for ablation, systemic therapy or active surveillance; partial nephrectomy preserves renal function.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: He has visible haematuria. When should the GP refer?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I'd send a urine sample and repeat it in a month before referring.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: CT shows the renal mass and a bladder defect. Anything else?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: No, the CT has shown both lesions, so we have the answer.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: What is the renal mass likely to be?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: A transitional cell carcinoma, like the bladder.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: Cystoscopy shows a papillary tumour. What next?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Biopsy it first, then a radical nephrectomy.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: A suspected cancer pathway referral: he is over 45 with unexplained visible haematuria and no infection.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Urine dipstick and culture, renal function, CT urography for the upper tracts and cystoscopy for the bladder.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: What are the lesions likely to be?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: The renal mass is likely a renal cell carcinoma, mostly clear cell. The bladder lesion is likely a urothelial carcinoma.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Smoking for both. Aromatic amines at work for the bladder; obesity and hypertension for the kidney.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: TURBT including detrusor muscle, with a single dose of mitomycin C, then treatment according to risk.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: MDT. Neoadjuvant cisplatin-based chemotherapy if he's fit for it, then radical cystectomy or radiotherapy with a radiosensitiser.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Stage with CT of the chest and abdomen, discuss at MDT, and partial nephrectomy for a T1 tumour if feasible.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: 45 or over with unexplained visible haematuria, or visible haematuria persisting after a treated urinary infection. Also 60 or over with non-visible haematuria and dysuria or a raised white count. The same visible-haematuria rule covers renal cancer.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Why does he need cystoscopy if the CT shows the bladder lesion?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: CT can miss flat lesions like carcinoma in situ, and I need tissue. Urine cytology or biomarkers don't replace cystoscopy.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Tell me about the renal pathology.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Clear cell RCC, linked to loss of the VHL gene on chromosome 3p. The other main types are papillary and chromophobe.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: He smokes, and as an industrial painter he may have had aromatic amine exposure. I'd also ask about von Hippel-Lindau syndrome in the family, and support him to stop smoking.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: The bladder tumour is high-risk non-muscle-invasive.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: He needs a repeat TURBT within 6 weeks. Then he'd choose between intravesical BCG, induction and maintenance, and radical cystectomy.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Stage with CT chest, abdomen and pelvis, and discuss urinary diversion with him and a clinical nurse specialist.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Should you biopsy the renal mass?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Not routinely. Biopsy is for ablation, systemic therapy or active surveillance. For a T1 tumour, partial nephrectomy preserves renal function.

failures.move: Stopping at CT urography and not arranging cystoscopy.
failures.consequence: Carcinoma in situ or further tumours are missed and no tissue diagnosis is made.

failures.move: Offering cystectomy before TURBT has shown the stage and grade.
failures.consequence: Major surgery for a tumour that TURBT and intravesical therapy may control.

failures.move: Going straight to cystectomy for muscle-invasive disease without MDT or neoadjuvant chemotherapy.
failures.consequence: He loses the survival benefit of chemotherapy and the choice of bladder-preserving radiotherapy.

failures.move: Repeating urine tests before referring visible haematuria.
failures.consequence: Delays the diagnosis of two cancers.

recovery.when: You said cystectomy is the only option
recovery.line: Muscle-invasive disease goes to the MDT: neoadjuvant chemotherapy, then cystectomy or radiotherapy with a radiosensitiser.

recovery.when: Asked for a percentage you are unsure of
recovery.line: I wouldn't quote a figure I can't source; smoking is the main risk factor for bladder cancer.

knowledge.fact: NG12: suspected cancer pathway referral for bladder or renal cancer at 45 or over with unexplained visible haematuria without infection, or persisting after treated infection.
Urinary biomarkers do not replace cystoscopy (NG2).
TURBT should include detrusor muscle; single intravesical mitomycin C at first TURBT.
High-risk non-muscle-invasive: choice of BCG (induction and maintenance) or radical cystectomy.
Muscle-invasive: neoadjuvant cisplatin-based chemotherapy, then radical cystectomy or radiotherapy with a radiosensitiser.
RCC: clear cell, papillary, chromophobe; stage with contrast CT chest and abdomen; partial nephrectomy for T1.
Smoking is the most important bladder cancer risk factor; aromatic amines next.

recall.think: Two cancers: the bladder needs cystoscopy and TURBT, the kidney needs staging.
recall.say: "Suspected cancer pathway referral, CT urography and cystoscopy."

numbers.meaning: Age for suspected cancer referral with visible haematuria

recall.trap: CT seeing a bladder lesion does not replace cystoscopy.
recall.finish: Bladder: TURBT, then BCG, or neoadjuvant chemotherapy with cystectomy or radiotherapy. Kidney: partial nephrectomy for T1.

partner.opening: This man has painless visible haematuria. CT urography shows a right renal mass and a bladder filling defect. When should he have been referred?

reveals.trigger: Candidate asks for urine and blood results
reveals.finding: Dipstick: blood 3+, nitrite negative. Culture: no growth. eGFR 72.
Single 2 cm papillary tumour on the left lateral wall; surrounding mucosa looks normal.

reveals.trigger: Candidate asks for the TURBT histology
reveals.finding: High-grade urothelial carcinoma, pT1; no detrusor muscle in the specimen.

reveals.trigger: Candidate asks about the renal mass stage
reveals.finding: Contrast CT: 3.5 cm solid enhancing right renal mass, no nodal or distant disease (cT1a).

push.question: What are the referral criteria for visible haematuria?
push.expect: 45 or over, unexplained, no infection or persisting after treatment: suspected cancer pathway.

push.question: Why does he need cystoscopy?
push.expect: CT misses flat lesions; need tissue; biomarkers don't replace it.

push.question: How is a high-risk non-muscle-invasive tumour treated?
push.expect: Repeat TURBT within 6 weeks; then BCG or radical cystectomy.

push.question: Is cystectomy the only option once it's muscle-invasive?
push.expect: No: MDT, neoadjuvant cisplatin chemotherapy, cystectomy or radiotherapy with a radiosensitiser.

curveballs.prompt: Should we just biopsy the renal mass to be sure?
curveballs.safeAnswer: Not routinely; biopsy if it would change management (ablation, systemic therapy, surveillance).

curveballs.prompt: His urine cytology is negative. Can we skip cystoscopy?
curveballs.safeAnswer: No: cytology and biomarkers do not replace cystoscopy.

curveballs.prompt: What percentage of bladder cancers are due to smoking?
curveballs.safeAnswer: Gives no figure without a source; states smoking is the most important risk factor.
